view: Exegetes differ whether Joseph's interpretation came from knowledge God taught him or from direct revelation; the unasked-for prediction of a further abundant year supports revelation.
note: Qatada says the first fertile and next drought years follow the dream, while God gave Joseph knowledge of the later abundant year.

view: A report says Joseph stockpiled harvests, then sold food during famine for money, valuables, livestock, servants, property, land, and finally freedom; he later freed the Egyptians and restored their possessions and kingship.
note: The report is attributed to al-Rida.

view: The author omits many similar reports about the famine economy because most do not directly aid interpretation of these verses.

Al-Qummi reports the king's dream of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean cows and green ears with dry ones; after a delay, the cupbearer recalled it, and Joseph interpreted plentiful years, famine years, then rain.

Al-Sadiq interprets the following year as a year of rain; a report gives the passive reading 'they are rained upon,' deriving the verb from rain rather than rescue, and al-Ayyashi transmits the same reading.
note: These notes concern the year after the seven severe years.

view: Joseph's reply combines interpretation of the dream by meaning rather than wording, practical advice, and a report about the unseen year after the famine.
The dream presents the practical measures needed for famine: repeated planting, preserving grain in its ears, and rationing reserves, rather than merely forecasting fertile and barren years.
note: Tabatabai rejects interpreters who read Joseph's words simply as a forecast of seven fertile and seven barren years.

view: The Qur'anic Joseph story illustrates God's hidden direction of human affairs: people may dislike what benefits them or love what harms them, unlike Genesis' romantic account of Joseph's fortunes.
note: The note cites 2:216.

view: Joseph's interpretation covers the next fifteen years of Egypt's agricultural cycle.
An unbeliever's dream can be true and interpreted as seen, especially when it concerns a believer; here it also serves as a sign and miracle for a messenger.
Saying 'after that' rather than 'after them' magnifies the preceding period.
The years are called severe because the people living through them suffer hardship.
note: Tabatabai prefers the competing sense of years that attack, because it fits the following image of devouring.

view: Shidda denotes severity, firmness, or difficulty; an account lists seven uses of the term, including time, anger, pain, drink, and the body.
Arabic descriptions of famine say a year strips everything bare and dries stars, meat, and bone.
The counted noun 'years' is omitted after 'seven severe ones' and understood from the preceding mention of seven years.
Calling the years severe is a rational metaphor: hardship occurs during them.
The severe years are pictured as attackers or ravenous predators that pounce and devour the stored food; this reading of 'severe' fits the following image of eating.
note: Tabatabai prefers this sense over severity as hardship for the people.

view: The lean cows and dry ears of the king's dream represent the seven barren or famine years; the fat cows represent fertile years, and ears of grain signify provisions.
note: Ibn Ashur explains agricultural years through cows' fatness and leanness.

view: Joseph recognized the first severe year when a man who normally left half of his food ate his whole portion; one report says Joseph prepared food for two.
note: The reports name Ibn Zayd or Zayd ibn Aslam and differ in how they describe the portion.

view: The Prophet prayed for Quraysh to experience seven years like Joseph's famine; the hardship began but ended before seven years.
Seven severe years of drought and famine follow the fertile years, bringing hardship to the people.
note: Some notes also identify the years with the dream's lean cows and dry ears; those symbols have a separate view.

view: The famine is harder for people to endure than captivity or killing.
The seven-year duration of the famine follows the imagery of the two dreams.
note: The note connects this interpretation with 12:36 and 12:43.

view: Eating can mean using up, wearing away, or destroying; Arabs say that a journey 'ate' a camel's flesh, and a verse by Dhu al-Rumma illustrates this use.
note: Ibn Ashur also cites Qur'an 4:2 for the sense of consumption.

view: Eating is attributed figuratively to the years, although their inhabitants actually eat the stored food during them. Poetry similarly attributes heedlessness to day and sleep to night.
note: The notes illustrate temporal attribution with day or night, including comparisons to 10:67, 27:86, and 40:61.

view: Describing the years as eating matches the dream's image of lean cows consuming fat cows.
note: Bursevi says the dream cows did not literally eat one another: the image means famine consumes stored grain.

view: Al-Sulami reads the verb as 'they eat' in the third person, referring to the people, instead of addressing the listeners.
The lean cows eating the fat cows picture famine using up the provisions produced during prosperous years; the seven dry ears signify provisions stored across seven years.
note: Tabatabai treats the cows as yearly provisions from sustained planting.

view: The famine years consume the food and grain stored from the fertile years in preparation for them.
note: The individual notes vary between 'food,' 'grain,' and 'provisions.'

view: The drought years yield nothing: whatever is sown brings no return, so people consume their earlier stores.
Joseph's plan lets successive stored harvests sustain the population through seven drought years, together with the scant produce obtained during the famine.
note: Study Quran notes that Joseph advised storing most of the first phase's harvest for the second phase.

view: What was put forward for the years means the crops or grain prepared and stored in advance for those years.
Al-Sadiq reports the revealed wording as 'what you bring near for them.'
Grain is left in its ear to keep better and resist spoilage while awaiting the severe drought years.
note: Tabatabai sees unthreshed grain in the dream's dry ears; Bursevi says grain was stored in its ears.

view: The wording urges ample stockpiling because the drought years will exhaust almost all stored provisions.
The passage permits storing food until it is needed.
The feminine pronoun for the years reinforces their personification or matches the imagery of the dream.
The green ears in the dream represent stores to save, while the dry ears indicate preserving grain unthreshed and the work needed to protect supplies.
Only a small remainder of the provisions escapes consumption and is kept in reserve.
The little saved is reserved as seed for sowing after the famine, safeguarding future provisions.
note: Mawardi presents the seed explanation as a further possibility; Tabatabai links the seed to the recovery year.

view: The reserve should last through the famine, while only a small amount is kept outside storage for immediate consumption.
note: This differs from the reading that the small preserved amount is seed for later planting.

view: The protected remnant serves as both a reserve and seed for the recovery year; the dream depicts lean cows eating fat cows without consuming every last one.
Qalīlan is accusative as an exception.
Tuḥṣinūn means to preserve, secure, guard, or store provisions; iḥṣān carries the sense of protection, as in placing something inside a fortress or guarded enclosure.
note: Al-Suddi's report says 'raise or save'; Abu Ubayda and Qatada give guarding and storing as equivalent senses.

view: The preserved provisions are kept in protected storehouses or granaries.
note: Mawardi presents this as a possible sense.
